## Results

To test hypotheses aimed at answering open questions about the evolution of mitogenomic architectures and sequences (Table 1 and Supplementary Note 1), we analysed 10,860 bilaterian mitogenomes, among which 5.2% were single-stranded, 3.6% belonged to macroparasitic species (ectoparasitic+endoparasitic), and 11.1% to species assigned to the low locomotory capacity category (Figure 1; Supplementary Table 2; Supplementary Data 1).

Ancestral mitogenomic architectures and strand distribution of genes

Hypothesis 1: On the basis of our own reconstruction of ancestral mitogenomic architectures and previous findings 5,30, the architecture identical to the one exhibited by most chordates, including humans (only PCGs and rRNAs were considered), was selected as the most likely ancestral architecture of all bilaterian animals (hypothesis 1a; Figure 1). This also implies that double-stranded architecture and negative GC skew on the plus strand are the ancestral bilaterian states. There was some instability in the exact position of nad6 across different analyses, but its location on the minus strand was inferred with high confidence (more details in Supplementary Note 2 and Supplementary Figs. 1-2). Ancestral double-strandedness was further corroborated by the Maximum Likelihood ancestral state reconstruction for the two architecture types. This analysis included tRNA genes (eight on the minus strand in the human mitogenome), and resolved the ancestral state for Bilateria as double-stranded with a probability of 0.9999 (hypothesis 1b).

The above ur-bilaterian architecture was used as the reference for subsequent gene order rearrangement analyses, and to infer the evolutionary history of mitogenomic strandedness shifts (double-stranded / single-stranded).

Hypothesis 2: a double-stranded architecture was inferred as the most likely ancestral state for Deuterostomia/Xenambulacraria and all belonging phyla with high confidence. We inferred one architectural evolutionary transition from genes encoded on both strands to all genes encoded on a single strand (henceforth “double-to-single”) in Xenacoelomorpha and at least one in Tunicata (Chordata), likely in the common ancestor of classes Thaliacea+Ascidiacea, but not Appendicularia. Details of these analyses are provided in Table 2 and Supplementary Note 3 and Supplementary Figs. 2-38. BayesTraits reconstruction produced double-stranded as the ancestral state for the superclade Protostomia and both of its superphyla, Ecdysozoa and Lophotrochozoa, with high probability (>0.999). Within the Ecdysozoa, double-stranded was inferred as the ancestral state for six out of seven phyla included in the dataset (Kinorhyncha was the outlier), and we inferred five putative double-to-single transitions. The superphylum Lophotrochozoa exhibited by far the most rearranged mitogenomic architectures and the most complex scenario of strandedness transitions. Likely due to the highly rearranged mitogenomic architectures of most lineages, we failed to reconstruct of the ancestral architecture for this superphylum with precision, but multiple sources of evidence indicate that a double-stranded architecture was the ancestral state. These comprise most results of the ancestral architecture reconstruction (Figure S8), BayesTraits reconstruction (probability of double-stranded > 0.999), and the fact that double-stranded was the most likely ancestral state for 11 out of 13 individual phyla, with Brachiopoda and Syndermata as the only exceptions. Syndermata comprise sensu-stricto phyla Acanthocephala (all single-stranded) and Rotifera (mostly single-stranded) (Figures S9-S12). We found indications of single-stranded to double-stranded transitions in several species of Rotifera, but due to their fragmented mitogenomes, within-species strandedness variability, and strand switches comprising only tRNA genes, these are not confirmed. Another double-to-single transition was inferred in Platyhelminthes after Catenulida branched-off. Three lophotrochozoan phyla exhibited particularly complex scenarios: Bryozoa, Annelida, and Mollusca. In Annelida we identified a double-to-single evolutionary shift after Palaeoannelida branched-off, followed by a state reversal (i.e. single-to-double shift) in a single derived Sedentaria species, Sabella spalanzani (Sabellidae). Finally, Mollusca exhibited the most complex scenario, with multiple putative shifts in strandedness, comprising several putative state reversals observed in the class Bivalvia (Table 2).

GORR values distribution

Hypothesis 3: GORR values in comparison to the ancestral bilaterian architecture ranged between 0 and 12 in the complete dataset (Figures 1 and 2). The distribution of GORR values across individual phyla could be roughly classified into three basic, albeit not necessarily mutually exclusive, patterns of architectural evolution. (1) Discontinuous: in most phyla, the ancestral architecture (disregarding volatile tRNA genes) for the phylum is highly conserved in a majority of species, with exponentially elevated rearrangement rates in a small proportion of species (e.g. Arthropoda, Chordata, Nematoda, and Echinodermata). (2) Episodic: mitogenomic architecture is re-stabilised after an evolutionary period of increased levels of architectural rearrangements, commonly occurring deep in the evolutionary history (e.g. Nematoda and Arthropoda). (3) Continuous: GORR values exhibit an approximately linear distribution, characterised by the absence of statistical outliers. Most phyla exhibited a combination of episodic and discontinuous patterns, whereas Mollusca and Bryozoa were the only phyla exhibiting a continuous pattern. In addition, Platyhelminthes exhibited a unique pattern, with parasitic Neodermata exhibiting a strongly episodic pattern (exceptionally highly rearranged, but mostly stable architecture: GORR=9), and predominantly free-living “turbellaria” exhibiting much less rearranged, but fast-evolving in an apparently continuous manner, pattern of GORR distribution (Figure 2 and Supplementary Fig. 39).

GORR values, branch length, and strand distribution of genes

Hypothesis 4: Mitogenomic architectural evolutionary rates (GORR) strongly varied among the superphyla: highly conserved in Deuterostomia (0.24), intermediate in Ecdysozoa (3.29), and high in Lophotrochozoa (6.86). In support of the working hypothesis. branch lengths followed this pattern, but with less pronounced differences (Supplementary Fig. 40). Congruent patterns across the two variables were also observed across the individual phyla, with the slowest evolution in Chordata, Hemichordata, and Echinodermata, and fastest in Platyhelminthes, Orthonectida, and Mollusca/Acanthocephala (GORR/branch length respectively) (Figure 1 and 2, Supplementary Table 2). As a result, the correlation between GORR and branch length was strong and positive in the overall dataset (hypothesis 4a; r=0.69; p<0.001; Figure 3A), and branch length variability explained 37 - 40% of the GORR variability in Bilateria (Table 3). As Chordata exhibited a unique evolutionary pattern, and represented a majority of the dataset, major hypotheses were additionally tested with Chordata removed from the dataset: the overall conclusions remained the same, although the correlation value between GORR and branch length was slightly reduced (0.57). Correlation between GORR and branch length was also positive (albeit mostly weak) in all individual phyla aside from Mollusca (-0.08) (Figure 3), as well as in mitogenomes with low rearrangement rates (GORR<7; r=0.69, R2=42-45%; rejecting the hypothesis 4b), and in the dataset split along the lines of architectural type: single-stranded (r=0.86, R2=66-70%) and double-stranded (r=0.70, R2=47-49%). Contrary to this, highly rearranged mitogenomes (GORR≥7) exhibited a very weak negative correlation (-0.18) between GORR and branch length, reflected in low explanatory power (R2=3%), but the pattern was restored when Mollusca were removed from this dataset (r=0.71, R2=51%; further details in Table 3; Supplementary Note 4, Figs. 41 - 44, and Data 2).

Hypothesis 5: Next, we tested the hypothesis that mitogenomes with all genes encoded on the same strand are exhibit signatures of relaxed purifying selection pressures compared to double-stranded mitogenomes. In agreement with the working hypothesis 5a, GORR values were significantly higher in single-stranded mitogenomes across the Bilateria (Figure 4A; p<0.001, details in Supplementary Data 3). At the level of individual phyla, results were inconsistent, with Chordata and Arthropoda exhibiting a congruent pattern, but Annelida and Nematoda exhibiting an inverted GORR pattern (Figure 4A). In support of the hypothesis 5b, single-stranded mitogenomes exhibited significantly higher sequence evolutionary rates across the Bilateria (Figure 4B; p<0.001). At the level of individual phyla, results were only partially consistent, with single-stranded lineages exhibiting significantly longer branches in Chordata and Mollusca, nonsignificantly longer in Annelida and Arthropoda, and Nematoda exhibiting an inverted pattern (Figure 4B). Both hypotheses were also confirmed when Chordata were removed from the dataset (Supplementary Fig. 45).

As regards GC skews, mitogenomes with inverted (positive) values were observed in almost all phyla, aside from three phyla represented by only a few specimens: Entoprocta (n=2), Hemichordata (n=6), and Nematomorpha (n=1) (Figure 4C and Supplementary Fig. 46). GC skews were predominantly negative (the ancestral state) in double-stranded mitogenomes, and predominantly positive in single-stranded mitogenomes, but there were multiple exceptions from this rule, with Annelida as a major outlier (+ in ds, - in ss). In agreement with the hypothesis 5c, the absolute skew magnitude was significantly higher in single-stranded than in double-stranded mitogenomes (confirmed in both Bilateria - Figure 5A, and Chordata - Supplementary Fig. 47).

GC skews and Ne

Hypothesis 6: contrary to the working hypothesis 6a, GC skew (│value│>0.1) was negatively weakly correlated with GORR (r=-0.25), with a negligible explanatory power (R2≈3%). However, the working hypothesis was weakly-moderately supported when we separately analysed Chordata and the remaining Bilateria (both r=0.38; all p=<0.001), with higher explanatory power values (R2≈26-28% and 16-17% respectively). Hypothesis 5b was also rejected in the Bilateria dataset, where the correlation between GC skew and branch length was negligible (r=0.13, R2<1%), but supported when we separately analysed Chordata (r=0.37, R2≈20%) and the remaining Bilateria (r=0.50; R2≈28%; p=<0.001 in all cases; Supplementary Fig. 48).

Hypothesis 7: the Ne dataset comprised 202 species, belonging to four phyla: Chordata (182 species), Mollusca (9), Arthropoda (8), and Echinodermata (3). All were free living, but all three locomotory capacity categories were represented: 180 species in high, 14 in intermediate, and 9 in low. There were four single-stranded mitogenomes in the dataset. Contrary to the working hypotheses 7a-c, Ne was not correlated with GORR (r=0.07, p=0.30; R2=0.010), branch length (r=0.03, p=0.66; R2<0.006), and GC skew (r=-0.14, p=0.05; R2≈0.030). It was also not associated with strandedness (R2<0.030) and with skew inversions (R2<0.005) (Supplementary Fig. 49 and Data 2).

Parasitism, locomotory capacity, and thermoregulatory type

Hypothesis 8: In agreement with the working hypothesis 8a, endoparasitic species exhibited by far the most highly rearranged mitogenomic architectures, followed by ectoparasites, parasitoids, micropredators, and free-living species (Figure 5B). In pairwise comparisons, all differences were statistically significant (Tukey HSD tests; details in Supplementary Data 3), and Bayes factors were huge (Figure 6A, Figure S50). Statistical power was good and effect sizes were very large or huge for key pairwise comparisons: endoparasites vs. free-living (Cohen’s d=2.6), and ectoparasites vs. free-living (1.5) (Figure 6B). The results were replicated with Chordata removed from the dataset and across the Ecdysozoa and Lophotrochozoa (Supplementary Fig. 45). The patterns across the individual phyla were congruent in Platyhelminthes, and partially congruent in Arthropoda (elevated GORR in ectoparasites but not in endoparasites) and Nematoda (GORR was nonsignificantly increased in endoparasites) (Supplementary Fig. 51), and mixed across lower taxonomic levels (class and order): consistent in Insecta, Chromadorea, Malacostraca, Hexanauplia, and Rhabditida, but not in Arachnida, Enoplea, and Diptera (Supplementary Figs. 52 and 53). While lmekin and brms analyses indicated that the division along the lifestyle lines (parasitism) explained only around 6% of the variability in GORR in the bilaterian dataset, these values were higher once Chordata were excluded from the dataset: ≈33% in Ecdysozoa, ≈16% in Lophotrochozoa, and ≈20% in Protostomia (Table 3; Supplementary Data 2). To reduce the effect of variability in locomotory capacity, we focused only on the low locomotory capacity category divided along the lifestyle lines (hypothesis 8b). The pattern produced by the overall bilaterian dataset was only partially upheld, with the highest GORR values exhibited by endoparasites, but ectoparasites exhibited a lower value than free-living (Figure 5C). The explanatory power remained similar to the one in the full dataset (≈8%, Table 3).

Hypothesis 8c: in support of the working hypothesis, the far end of the positive GC skew distribution was marked by the strong prevalence of endoparasites: 24 species with highest skews were all endoparasites, and among the top 100 species with highest skews (GC range = 0.477 – 0.684), 93 were endoparasitic. A similar pattern was observed at the negative end of the GC skew distribution, where four highest values were exhibited by endoparasites (18 endoparasites in total in the GC-negative dataset). In partial agreement with these observations and the working hypothesis, absolute GC skews were the highest in endoparasites, but ectoparasites and parasitoids exhibited lower average values than the free-living species (Figure 5D, Supplementary Fig. S47). In support of hypothesis 8d, we found an increased likelihood (>37×) of skew inversions (positive GC skew) in macroparasitic (ectoparasitic+endoparasitic) species compared to free living (p<0.001, Fisher’s test, one-sided; Supplementary Fig. 54), with life history explaining 22% of the variability in skew direction (plus or minus).

Finally, in support of the hypothesis 8e, we found an increased likelihood of single-stranded mitogenomes in endoparasitic (>17×) and ectoparasitic (>3×) species , and decreased in other categories (<0.6× in free-living; Figure 7). Also, there was a highly significant association between life history and strandedness (p<0.001, Chi-square test of independence; Supplementary Data 3), with life history explaining 38-41% of the variability in the distribution of strand types across lineages (Table 3).

Hypothesis 9: in agreement with the working hypothesis 9a, GORR values were significantly increased in the low locomotory capacity category (Figure 5E). For the high vs. low category comparison, Bayes Factor was huge (Figure 6A, Supplementary Fig. 50), statistical power was good, and the effect size was huge (Cohen’s d=2.8; Figure 6C). The results were replicated with Chordata removed from the dataset and across all but one major taxonomic clades when both categories were present in sufficient numbers (n≥3): superphyla (Ecdysozoa+Lophotrochozoa), phyla (Chordata, Arthropoda, and Mollusca), and classes (Insecta, Malacostraca, and Arachnida) (insufficient data at the order level). The class Hexanauplia was the only major lineage where the hypothesis was rejected (Supplementary Figs. 45, 55, and 56). The explanatory power of locomotory capacity categorisation on GORR variability was ≈14% in Bilateria, ≈11% in Lophotrochozoa, and 33% in Ecdysozoa (Table 3). To remove the effect of parasitism on the locomotory capacity classification, we conducted analyses using only free-living species (hypothesis 9b). The pattern observed in the full dataset was mostly fully upheld (Figure 5F), and the explanatory power was ≈11% (Table 3). Among the ectoparasites (hypothesis 9c), those with low locomotory capacity had strongly (1.6×) but non-significantly increased GORR values (Figure 5G). In support of hypothesis 9d, GC skews were significantly increased in low-locomotory species (Figure 5H). In support of hypothesis 9e, there was an increased likelihood (>99×) of skew inversions (positive GC skew) in low-locomotory category compared to the high-locomotory category species (p<0.001, Fisher’s test, one-sided; Figure S54), and locomotory capacity explained 47% of the variability in skew direction. In support of hypothesis 9f, we found an increased likelihood (>3×) of single-stranded mitogenomes in species classified into the low locomotory capacity category, and decreased among the high-locomotory species (<0.4×, Figure 7, Supplementary Data 3). There was a highly significant association between the locomotory capacity and strandedness (p ≈ 0.0, Chi-square test of independence), with locomotory capacity explaining ≈33% of the variability in strand types across lineages (Table 3).

Hypothesis 10: in the bilaterian dataset 8,498 species were ectotherms, and 2,362 were endotherms (all Chordata and almost all free-living). Among the endotherms, >99% were classified in the high locomotory capacity category (none were low-locomotory). Among the ectotherms, ≈75% were high-locomotory, and ≈14% were low-locomotory. In agreement with the working hypotheses 10a/b, ectotherms exhibited significantly higher GORR (hypothesis 10a, Figure 5I), and branch lengths (hypothesis 10b, Figure 5J) than ectotherms, but Chordata exhibited an inverted pattern (Supplementary Fig. 45). The explanatory power of thermoregulatory type on these two variables was small: ≈2% and ≈5%, respectively (Table 3). Contrary to the working hypothesis 10c, endotherms exhibited significantly higher average GC skew value than ectotherms (both across the Bilateria and only Chordata; Figure 5K and Supplementary Fig. 47).

Mitogenome size patterns and correlates

Hypothesis 11: Aside from hypothesis 11i, all other hypotheses associated with correlates of mitogenomic size were rejected. Mitogenomes were the smallest (≈12.6 Kb) in Longidoridae (Nematoda: Enoplea), and the largest in two Bivalvia (Mollusca) species: Anadara sativa (48.2 Kb) and Dreissena rostriformis (46.7 Kb). Only eight species exhibited mitogenomes >30 Kb (5 Mollusca and 3 Arthropoda). Multiple Chordata species (Squamata and Anura) were among the largest mitogenomes (>25 Kb) (Supplementary Data 1). The correlation between GORR and mitogenome size was weakly/moderately negative in Bilateria (hypothesis 11a; r=-0.39, Figure 3B), and size explained ≈10% of the GORR variability (Table 3). In individual phyla, correlation between GORR and size was highly variable: positive in Annelida, Echinodermata, and Nematoda (weak – moderate); negative in Platyhelminthes and Mollusca (weak); and negligible in Arthropoda, Chordata, and Bilateria (Figure 3B, Supplementary Fig. 57). The correlation between mitogenome size and branch length was weakly negative across the bilaterian dataset (hypothesis 11b, r=-0.33, Figure 3C). It also varied across the individual phyla: positive in Mollusca, Nematoda, Echinodermata, and Annelida (weak – moderate); negative in Arthropoda and Platyhelminthes (negligible – weak); and negligible in Chordata and Bilateria (Figure 3C, Supplementary Fig. 57). Ne values were not correlated with size (hypothesis 11c, r=-0.09, p=0.21, R2<0.013, Supplementary Fig. 49). GC skew was also negligibly correlated with size across all tested datasets (hypothesis 11d, r≈-0.07 - 0.17; R2≈0.005 - 0.030; Table 3, Supplementary Fig. 48). Mitogenomes were the largest in free-living, and the smallest in ectoparasitic and endoparasitic lineages (hypothesis 11e, Figure 5L). Mitogenomes were larger in high-locomotory than in low-locomotory categories (hypothesis 11f, Figure 5M). Double-stranded mitogenomes were larger than single-stranded ones (hypothesis 11g, Figure 5N). Endotherms had larger mitogenomes than ectotherms (hypothesis 11h, Figure 5O). Finally, in agreement with hypothesis 11i, variability in size was lesser in endotherms than in ectotherms (SD = 537 vs. 1340, respectively, Figure 5O).

## Methods

Dataset, categorisation, phylogeny, branch lengths, and Ne

Features of all mitogenomes of bilaterian animals available in the NCBI’s manually curated RefSeq database were extracted, calculated, and comparative tables generated using PhyloSuite 75,76. The dataset was categorised according to the lifestyle (endoparasites, ectoparasites, parasitoids, micropredators, and free-living species), locomotory capacity (high, intermediate, and low), and thermoregulatory type (endotherms and ectotherms). Duplicated genes were resolved using PhyloSuite following the methodology described previously 10,75. To infer branch lengths, we used the phylogeny from our previous study 10, reconstructed using concatenated amino acid sequences of 12 mitochondrial protein-coding genes (atp8 removed) of all mitogenomes in the dataset, and mtZOA+G4+F+C50 model in IQ-TREE v2.2.0.7.mix 77. We constrained the phylum-level topology according to the bilaterian phylogeny in Laumer et al.78, with Xenacoelomorpha as the sister lineage to all other bilaterians 79,80 (“Nephrozoa” topology henceforth). The molecular sequence evolution rate was defined as the root-to-tip branch lengths, which were extracted using the TreeSuite function in PhyloSuite. More details about the dataset, including the limitations of these classifications, and methodology are available in Supplementary Methods and in Jakovlić et al.10. The effective population size (Ne) analyses were extracted by overlapping the species in our dataset with those in the dataset recently compiled by Clarke et al.81. When there were multiple populations per species, we inferred average Ne values.

GC skews

To exclude the confounding factor of variability in the noncoding region size, GC skews were calculated 82 by PhyloSuite using only coding sections of the plus strand (GC skew is more pronounced than AT skew and thus more suitable for testing these hypotheses). To attempt to reduce the amount of noise in the GC skew dataset stemming from inversions in mutational pressures caused by inversions of the origin of replication 35,36 and facilitate the analysis of magnitude irrespective of skew direction, all GC skews were converted to their absolute values. To further reduce the amount of noise, the lower end of distribution (GC<0.1) was removed, as such low GC values commonly suggest ORI inversions or otherwise disrupted replication mechanisms, so they poorly reflect the strength of purifying selection pressure 36. In addition, we attempted to remove all annotation artefacts caused by the authors submitting the wrong mitogenomic strand to the GenBank via a manual inspection of the dataset (removed 65 species).

Mitogenomic architecture analyses

Mitogenomes of bilaterian animals commonly encode 37 genes (13 protein-coding genes - PCGs, 2 rRNAs, and 22 tRNAs) distributed in varying arrangements across both DNA strands, by convention named “plus” and “minus”. This arrangement is referred to as mitogenomic architecture, and it can be quantified as the gene order rearrangement rate (GORR). For the ancestral architecture inference, we relied on previous proposals of ancestral architectures for different lineages (Supplementary Table 3), and conducted the ancestral mitogenomic architecture inference using TreeREx 83 and MLGO 84 using a linearised gene order dataset from which tRNAs were removed due to their highly variable content and difficulties in annotation. To minimise the noise and reduce the size of dataset (362 species after the reduction), we used only the ancestral architecture for a phylum when it was inferred with confidence by previous studies (e.g. only the mitogenome of Homo sapiens for Chordata 5,30 and Limulus polyphemus for Arthropoda 85), and only the “basal” lineage of large phyla exhibiting high rearrangement rates (e.g. only Catenulida for Platyhelminthes 57). As the phylogeny of Bilateria remain debated, we tested two topologies, both constrained at the phylum level. Aside from the “Nephrozoa” topology, described in the first section, we also tested the topology where Xenacoelomorpha is the sister group to Ambulacraria (Hemichordata+Echinodermata) 86,87, with paraphyletic Deuterostomia 88 - named “Xenambulacraria” henceforth. As this topology implies that the common ancestor of Chordata and Xenambulacraria (Ambulacraria+Xenacoelomorpha) was the last common ancestor of all Bilateria, and characters common to these two clades would be bilaterian plesiomorphies 88, we removed the highly rearranged Protostomia (Ecdysozoa and Lophotrochozoa) 5,30, and tested a dataset comprising only the outgroups, Xenambulacraria, and Chordata, constrained according to the relationships proposed previously 86,88. The outgroups were Cnidaria, Porifera, and Placozoa. Further methodological details are provided in Supplementary Methods. The inferred ur-bilaterian mitogenomic architecture (tRNAs excluded) was then used to calculate mitogenomic GORR values using the Breakpoint Distance measure in CREX 89. As TreeREx and CREX cannot handle missing genes, for these analyses, atp8 was removed from all mitogenomes, and species with further missing PCGs or rRNAs were removed from these analyses, which included the entire phylum Chaetognatha - lacking atp6 2,90. In addition, all mitogenomes were classified into two categories according to the strand distribution of genes: double-stranded (genes encoded on both strands) and single-stranded (all genes encoded on a single strand), and then the Maximum Likelihood method in BayesTraits v4.0.1 91 was used to infer the ancestral states of strand distribution of genes. To get a better resolution for strandedness analyses, we further analysed complete GenBank mitogenomic datasets (as opposed to only RefSeq) for all poorly represented major lineages, and for all lineages with complex evolutionary histories.

Statistical analyses

As GORR values equalled 0 for more than half of the dataset, mostly due to a majority of Chordata having a perfectly conserved ancestral bilaterian architecture and being overrepresented in the dataset (>50% of all species), we recoded GORR=0 values to 0.0000001 for all statistical analyses. To further confirm that Chordata did not skew our statistical analyses, we additionally tested all major hypotheses using a bilaterian dataset from which all Chordata were removed. Outliers in GORR distributions were identified using the IQR method (InterQuartile Range), selected due to the non-normality of GORR distribution. Pairwise comparisons of between different groups were conducted using Tukey HSD tests in the R package agricolae v1.3.5 92. As the limitations of the traditional p-value-based statistics are well-documented, we further assessed the reliability of statistical analyses by employing multiple recommended alternative tests 93. Effect sizes were inferred using the R package efsize. Statistical power analyses were conducted for each effect size measure using the pwr.t2n.test method in the R package pwr. Herein, power refers to the probability of detecting a statistically significant effect if one exists, and the commonly accepted cut-off value for a good statistical power is ≥ 0.8. Bayesian hypothesis testing was conducted using BayesFactor 94. As the dataset violated the assumption of independence of data, two algorithms designed to account for phylogenetic relatedness were used to conduct multilevel linear regression analyses: linear fixed-effect models accounting for kinship implemented in the lmekin function in coxme v2.2.16 95, and phylogenetic multilevel Bayesian models implemented in brms v2.16.150 96. For these analyses, we used a matrix of phylogenetic distances extracted from the phylogenetic tree described above using the ape v5.5 package 97. The R2 value of lmekin models was calculated using the r.squaredLR method available in the MuMIn v1.46.0 package in R. The Bayesian R2 value was inferred using the bayes_r2 function of brms package in R. For brms and lmekin analyses, we log-transformed the obtained GORR data to reduce the non-normality of distribution. Pearson’s correlation coefficients (r) were inferred using R. Correlation values were classified as follows: negligible (<0.2), weak (0.2-0.4), moderate (0.4-0.6), strong (0.6-0.8), very strong (>0.8). Due to the very large number of samples in our study (>10,000), we did not rely on p-values to assess the support for the working hypotheses in correlation tests, as statistical tests are practically always highly significant on such high numbers of samples 98. Unless if specified otherwise, statistical tests were inherently two-sided.

optimization across diverse temperatures in ectotherms versus more stable ranges in endotherms.

other genomic and organismal traits.

relationships often include numerous exceptions. Incorporating strand skew and replication architecture could help interpret

statistical patterns to biological hypotheses would improve the interpretative strength of the study.

framed as correlations among categorical variables rather than tests of explicit, biologically motivated hypotheses.

### Reviewer 2

This manuscript presents a comprehensive analysis of mitogenomic architecture evolution across Bilateria, leveraging a
dataset of over 10,000 mitogenomes. The study addresses several unresolved questions regarding gene order
rearrangements, strandedness transitions, and correlations with lifestyle and locomotory capacity. The work is well-
structured, methodologically robust, and provides significant insights into mitogenomic evolution. However, some areas
require clarification or additional analysis to strengthen the conclusions.
Major Comments
1. Ancestral State Reconstruction
- The inference of the ancestral bilaterian mitogenomic architecture as double-stranded is well-supported, but the instability
in "nad6" positioning across analyses warrants further discussion. Could this instability reflect methodological limitations
(e.g., alignment ambiguity or model sensitivity)? A deeper exploration of alternative topologies (e.g., Xenambulacraria vs.
Nephrozoa) and their impact on ancestral state inference would strengthen the conclusions. The authors may want include a
sensitivity analysis to assess the robustness of the ancestral state.
2. Single- to Double-Stranded Transitions
- The identification of rare single-to-double-stranded transitions in Annelida and Mollusca challenges the "ratchet"
hypothesis. However, the evidence for these transitions (e.g., Sabella spalanzani) is based on limited taxa. Could annotation
artifacts or incomplete lineage sampling explain these observations?
3. Mitogenome Size and Evolutionary Rates
- The negative correlation between mitogenome size and evolutionary rates contradicts the "race for replication"
hypothesis. The proposed explanations are plausible but speculative.
4. Parasitism and Locomotory Capacity
- While the model linking low locomotory capacity to relaxed purifying selection is compelling, the explanatory power of
these variables for GORR variability is modest (6–14%). Other factors (e.g., effective population size, recombination rates)
may play significant roles. A discussion of how neutral processes might interact with selection might help.
5. Population size of mitochondrion may substantially different from the Ne of species.
---
Minor Comments
1. Statistical Analyses
- The use of phylogeny-corrected models (lmekin, brms) is appropriate, but the R² values for some comparisons (e.g., 3% for
GORR≥7/ds) are very low. Emphasize that these results suggest additional undetected factors drive architectural evolution.
2. Outliers
- The exceptional conservation in Cirripedia (Hexanauplia) is intriguing. The hypothesis of large effective population size is
untested. Could life-history traits (e.g., sessility, larval dispersal) also contribute?
3. Supplementary Material
- Not all supplementary figures/tables are directly cited in the main text.

(Harvey et al. 2000; Luong and Mathot 2019). We should note that our initial analyses indicated that they exhibit almost
the same branch lengths as strictly endoparasitic nematodes. Contrary to this, we did not remove necromenic
Caenorhabditis species from the dataset because necromeny of these nematodes does not fit the definition of parasitism
employed in our classification, outlined at the beginning of this section: “…a consumer interaction in which the consumer
feeds on a single live individual (the host) during at least one life-history stage, where both parasites and hosts belong to
the Animalia…”. As necromenic dauer juveniles of nematodes simply remain on the body of the associated animal until it
dies, and then feed, further develop, and propagate on the decomposing cadaver (Kiontke and Sudhaus 2006), they do not
feed on the live host. This could be considered a form of non-feeding symbiosis, and it does not differ substantially from
phoresy (Kiontke and Sudhaus 2006), where dauer juveniles of nematodes use the associated animal only as a means of
transportation to carry them to a new food source (e.g. a carrion of a different animal).
Parasitic species with free-living life stages were a major problem in our classification, as many parasitic lineages have a life
stage that takes place outside the host. In most cases, however, it is the early life stages that are free-living (such as the
egg or some early larval form), and to our knowledge a vast majority of these have a very limited locomotory ability.
Finally, all of them have the adult stage that matures within the host. As this is in stark contrast to parasitoids, where the
larva is parasitic, whereas the adults are free-living and highly locomotory, we ultimately decided to
categorise all these species as parasitic, despite the complexity of their life-cycles, and the potential noise that it may introduce in our analyses.
Categorisation of locomotory capacity
The categorisation of locomotory capacity was based on the “visual interaction hypothesis”, which is the best explanatory
variable for variability in scaling coefficients between the mass-specific metabolic rate in marine animals: high metabolic
demand follows strong selection for locomotory capacity for pursuit and evasion in visual prey/predators inhabiting well-lit
oceanic waters, whereas limited visibility allows for reduced locomotory capacity, reflected in low metabolic rates
(Childress and Mickel 1985; Seibel and Drazen 2007). We divided the dataset into three locomotory capacity categories: (1)
High comprised all species expected to rely on locomotion for pursuit and evasion of prey/predators. This category
comprised a vast majority of species (8,713); (2) Low comprised all species that have merely a rudimentary locomotory
capacity. This comprises sedentary species, or those capable only of minimal, very slow locomotion, that do not rely on
locomotion for pursuit and evasion of prey/predators. This category comprised 1,202 species, mostly from lineages such as
nematodes, flatworms, sessile molluscs and crustaceans, parasitic crustaceans, ticks, some annelids, mites,
Acanthocephala, Diplura, Brachiopoda, Bryozoa, Ascidiacea, Echinodermata, Entoprocta, Gastrotricha, Gnathostomulida,
Hemichordata, Kinorhyncha, Nemertea, Onychophora, Orthonectida, Phoronida, Priapulida, Tardigrada, and
Xenacoelomorpha; (3) Because locomotory capacity is a continuous trait, it is impossible to categorise species into only two
categories without creating a large overlap between the two categories. Therefore, to minimise the overlap between the
Low and High locomotory capacity categories, we designed a third category: Intermediate locomotory capacity. This
category comprised 945 species that would be expected to possess more than a rudimentary locomotory capacity, but also
rely on strategies other than locomotion to evade/pursue predators/prey. Examples are certain flightless insects and
Collembola, certain bathyal, abyssal and stygobitic crustacean and fish lineages, Chaetognatha, certain amphibian and
reptilian lineages, some mammals, some Bivalvia and Cephalopoda, some Gastropoda, Nematomorpha, and Rotifera.
Certain lineages were rather difficult to classify. Chaetognaths swim in short bursts using a dorso-ventral undulating body
motion, where their tail fin assists with propulsion and the body fins with stabilization and steering, so we classified them
into the Intermediate category. Among the Annelida, Sipuncula merely have a rudimentary LOC, so they were classified as
Low. Crassiclitellata (earthworms), Hirudinida (leeches) and Eunicida are capable of more than rudimentary locomotion, so
we classified them as Intermediate. Sabellida are sedentary, so we classified them as Low. Terebellida and Urechidae
appear to possess merely a rudimentary locomotory capacity, so we placed them into the Low category. Magelonidae are
burrowing worms with limited mobility, so we classified them as Low. Among the Nemertea, some species may possess
more than a basic locomotory capacity, but due to limited evidence, we classified them all as Low. Phoronida, Priapulida,
Entoprocta, and Hemichordata possess merely a rudimentary locomotory capacity, so all were classified as Low.
Onychophora can move at up to 5 cm per second, so we classified them as Intermediate.

Mitochondrial genomes of some animals remained almost unchanged architecturally for over half a billion of years, while other lineages exhibit conspecific variability. The drivers underlying this disparity remain unknown. We analyse over 10,000 bilaterian mitogenomes to test whether locomotory capacity and parasitic lifestyle can explain the variability in architectural evolutionary rates, and attempt to answer multiple other evolutionary questions. Double-stranded (genes on both strands) architecture is the most likely ancestral state for most major radiations (phylum and above). We identify over twenty transitions to single-stranded architectures, and the evidence of state-reversals (in Annelida and Mollusca). Gene order rearrangement and sequence evolution rates are positively correlated (r=0.69), and both are increased in single-stranded mitogenomes, parasites, and species with low locomotory capacity. The latter two categories exhibit increased prevalence of single-strandedness and GC skew inversions. Mitogenome size is negatively correlated with evolutionary rates, whereas the effective population size is decoupled from all tested evolutionary variables. Endotherms exhibit slower evolutionary rates than ectotherms in Bilateria, but faster in Chordata. Here, we provide evidence that purifying selection mediated by locomotory capacity and species ecology is a major driver of mitogenomic architectural evolution, but other variables are required to fully explain the observed patterns.

## Introduction

Mitogenomic architectural rearrangement rates, i.e. changes in the order and strand distribution of genes encoded by the animal mitochondrial genomes, vary dramatically among bilaterian lineages, but factors underlying this disparity in architectural evolutionary rates remain poorly understood 1–3. On the conserved end of the spectrum, most species of Chordata exhibit a mitogenomic architecture that remained almost unchanged over half a billion years 1,4,5. In contrast to this, some lineages of Mollusca, Isopoda, and Nematoda exhibit within-family/genus architectural variability 2,6–9, and nematodes from the family Mermithidae even exhibit conspecific architectural variability 7. Such stasis in the architectural evolution over long time spans is an indicator that architectural rearrangements are commonly deleterious, and likely disrupting mitogenomic replication, transcription, and gene expression co-regulation 1–3. However, no known models explain this apparent disparity in the stringency of selective constraints among lineages.

Recently, we have shown that parasitism and locomotory capacity have the power to explain a major proportion of variability in mitogenomic sequence evolutionary rates across the Bilateria 10. We proposed that reduction in energy demands allows reduced (ATP) production, which results in relaxation of purifying selection pressures – i.e. increased accumulation of deleterious mutations and accelerated evolutionary rates. Reduction in locomotory capacity and high metabolic dependence on the host (“auxotrophy”) characterise many parasitic animals, resulting in disproportionately elevated evolutionary rates, particularly in endoparasites 10. Based on that finding, and the fact that isolated parasitic lineages exhibit highly unusual, “disrupted”, rapidly evolving mitogenomic architectures 7–9,11–13, we hypothesised that parasitism and locomotory capacity variability may also have the power to explain the variability in architectural evolution.

As this hypothesis posits purifying selection pressure as the central mediator, it implies that architectural rearrangement rates (commonly quantified as gene order rearrangement rates - GORR) and sequence evolution (quantified as branch length) should exhibit a positive correlation. While some studies found support for this hypothesis 9,14–18, others found no correlation in isolated lineages 1,19,20. Some studies proposed that GORR and branch length are correlated only in lineages with high rearrangement rates, and not in those with low rearrangement rates 1,14, but this hypothesis remains untested statistically.

As regards parasitism, studies of its putative association with mitogenomic architecture evolution are scarce and results inconsistent: no correlation in Diptera (Insecta) 21, inconsistent results in Hymenoptera (Insecta) 22,23, no correlation in Annelida 18, and a recent study of Platyhelminthes found decreased GORR rates in parasites 20. Aside from a few sporadic mentions of this putative association 1,24–26, no other study had attempted to test it systematically. Our own studies of mitogenomes of parasitic animals (Supplementary Table 1) indicate that isolated lineages of nematodes and crustaceans do exhibit rapidly evolving architectures 8,9,11,27, but parasitic flatworms (Neodermata) exhibit comparatively slow-evolving architectures 28. As regards the hypothesis that species with low locomotory capacity should exhibit increased GORR rates, to our knowledge, it remains untested.

Several other questions regarding the correlates and patterns of mitogenomic evolution remain open. The observation that some species exhibit disproportionately rapid architectural evolutionary rates has produced a hypothesis that mitogenomic architecture evolution is “discontinuous”; i.e. that once a rearrangement event has destabilized the mitogenomic architecture, this is often followed by a cascade of rearrangements 11. Conversely, several comparative analyses suggested that architectural evolution is often re-stabilised after a burst of rearrangements 9,18,20, indicating an “episodic” evolutionary pattern, where purifying selection pressure is restored. Overall, the dynamics of architectural evolutionary rates remains poorly understood.

Further, mitogenomes can have genes encoded on both strands ("double-stranded") or on only one strand ("single-stranded")2. Boore4 proposed that evolutionary transitions from double-stranded to single-stranded architectures may be irreversible if they are accompanied by the loss of regulatory elements on the noncoding strand (“ratchet mechanism”). The evolutionary history of mitogenomic strandedness has never been systematically studied in animals, so the total number of state switches remains unknown, and the “ratchet” hypothesis untested. Even the ancestral state for bilaterians is debated, with some studies proposing a single-stranded ancestral architecture 2,29, whereas both studies that attempted to systematically infer the ancestral bilaterian (ur-bilaterian) architecture settled on a vertebrate-like double-stranded architecture 5,30.

A correlation between single-strandedness and highly rearranged mitogenomic architectures was proposed 2, but not tested statistically. We also noticed that some of the fastest mitogenomic DNA sequence evolutionary rates are exhibited by parasitic lineages that have exclusively or predominantly single-stranded architectures, such as Neodermata (Platyhelminthes), Chromadorea (Nematoda), and Acanthocephala 10. This is not a rule, as parasitic Orthonectida and Enoplea (Nematoda) exhibit both highly elevated evolutionary rates and double-stranded architectures 2,10,31. We hypothesise that single-strandedness may be an accidental consequence of relaxed purifying selection pressures allowing a wider range of rearrangement types, thus increasing the likelihood of a rearrangement producing a single-stranded architecture, which may then become fixed via the ratchet mechanism. This implies that single-stranded lineages should exhibit elevated sequence and architectural evolutionary rates, and be more common in parasitic and low-locomotory species.

Compositional asymmetry between strands (GC/AT skew) is linked to mitogenomic architecture via asymmetrical mutational pressures 32. Metabolic rate should be positively associated with GC skew magnitude via mutagenic reactive oxygen species 33, but crustaceans exhibited a negative correlation between these two variables, mediated by purifying selection driven by locomotory capacity variability 34. This suggests the existence of a positive correlation between GC skew and both GORR and branch length, as well as increased average GC skew values in single-stranded mitogenomes, parasites, and low-locomotory lineages. Aside from the association between GC skew and GORR in Annelida 18, and elevated GC skews in parasitic crustaceans 34, the universality of these hypotheses remains untested. Certain types of architectural rearrangements may change the direction of replication and transcription, thus changing the direction of mutational pressures, and eventually cause skew inversions 35. These have been identified in several phyla, and associated with increased branch lengths 1,35–37 and increased dN/dS ratios in crustaceans 36. Along with other arguments outlined herein, this suggests that skew inversions should be more likely in lineages evolving under relaxed selection pressures, i.e. parasitic and low-locomotory species.

Mitogenomic size is another variable that exhibits pronounced variability among bilaterian species for unknown reasons. Most animal mitogenomes evolve under a strong selection for small size, putatively driven by the “race for replication”, wherein smaller mitogenomes are replicated at higher rates due to their shorter replication time 38,39. This selection pressure should be more pronounced in species with high metabolic rates due to their faster mitogenomic metabolism and higher mitogenomic replication rates 39, implying that mitogenomes should be larger in species evolving under relaxed purifying selection pressures, and mitogenome size thus positively correlated with GORR, branch length and GC skew. Indirect support for the negative correlation between size and purifying selection was observed in some geckos and frogs 40. However, increased metabolic rates were not associated with smaller mitogenomes in selected tetrapod lineages 41. Aside from the supporting evidence for positive correlation between GORR and mitogenomic size in flatworms 20, correlates of mitogenomic size have not been tested statistically on a comprehensive dataset.

The above hypothesis also implies that mitogenomic size should be affected by the thermoregulation type: endotherms should have smaller mitogenomes and reduced size variability compared to ectotherms via their higher energy expenditure driving higher metabolic rates and producing a stronger race for replication 39,42. Support for this hypothesis was found on a dataset comprising mostly vertebrates and a small number of invertebrates 39. Further, two different models proposed that ectotherms should exhibit lower sequence mutation rates: the “functional constraints” hypothesis proposes that variations in the thermic environment may restrict physiologically acceptable amino acid substitutions 42,43, and the ”metabolic rate” hypothesis links the reduction in energy expenditure in ectotherms to a reduction in metabolic rates, production of mutagenic reactive oxygen species, and finally DNA mutation rates 33,42. Indeed, there is strong evidence that ectotherms exhibit significantly lower evolutionary rates than endotherms among vertebrates 33,42–44, and there is some evidence that the effect of thermoregulatory type remains consistent when invertebrates are included 45. However, this contradicts our central premise that high energy expenditure (as in endotherms) strengthens purifying selection. Indeed, vertebrates (which comprise all endothermic animals) exhibit some of the shortest branches among all bilaterians 10. Therefore, our working hypotheses contradict the proposals of reduced evolutionary rates in ectotherms, and instead propose reduced rates in endotherms, expected to be reflected in lower branch lengths, GC skew, and GORR.

Finally, a reduction in the effective population size (Ne) weakens the purifying selection 46–48, so we hypothesised that lower Ne should be reflected in higher average branch lengths, GORR values, GC skews, and mitogenome sizes 3,10,34,47. However, previous studies produced contradictory results 34,40,49–54, so the effects of Ne on mitogenomic evolution remain debated.

Herein, we rely on a mitogenomic dataset comprising almost 11,000 bilaterian species, categorised by locomotory capacity and lifestyle and assembled for our recent study 10, to test the hypotheses concerning the correlates of mitogenomic evolution outlined in this section, and provide evidence that purifying selection mediated by locomotory capacity and species ecology is a major driver of mitogenomic architectural evolution. However, analyses indicate that other variables must be invoked to fully explain observed patterns.

## Results

To test hypotheses aimed at answering open questions about the evolution of mitogenomic architectures and sequences (Table 1 and Supplementary Note 1), we analysed 10,860 bilaterian mitogenomes, among which 5.2% were single-stranded, 3.6% belonged to macroparasitic species (ectoparasitic+endoparasitic), and 11.1% to species assigned to the low locomotory capacity category (Figure 1; Supplementary Table 2; Supplementary Data 1).

Ancestral mitogenomic architectures and strand distribution of genes

Hypothesis 1: On the basis of our own reconstruction of ancestral mitogenomic architectures and previous findings 5,30, the architecture identical to the one exhibited by most chordates, including humans (only PCGs and rRNAs were considered), was selected as the most likely ancestral architecture of all bilaterian animals (hypothesis 1a; Figure 1). This also implies that double-stranded architecture and negative GC skew on the plus strand are the ancestral bilaterian states. There was some instability in the exact position of nad6 across different analyses, but its location on the minus strand was inferred with high confidence (more details in Supplementary Note 2 and Supplementary Figs. 1-2). Ancestral double-strandedness was further corroborated by the Maximum Likelihood ancestral state reconstruction for the two architecture types. This analysis included tRNA genes (eight on the minus strand in the human mitogenome), and resolved the ancestral state for Bilateria as double-stranded with a probability of 0.9999 (hypothesis 1b).

The above ur-bilaterian architecture was used as the reference for subsequent gene order rearrangement analyses, and to infer the evolutionary history of mitogenomic strandedness shifts (double-stranded / single-stranded).

Hypothesis 2: a double-stranded architecture was inferred as the most likely ancestral state for Deuterostomia/Xenambulacraria and all belonging phyla with high confidence. We inferred one architectural evolutionary transition from genes encoded on both strands to all genes encoded on a single strand (henceforth “double-to-single”) in Xenacoelomorpha and at least one in Tunicata (Chordata), likely in the common ancestor of classes Thaliacea+Ascidiacea, but not Appendicularia. Details of these analyses are provided in Table 2 and Supplementary Note 3 and Supplementary Figs. 2-38. BayesTraits reconstruction produced double-stranded as the ancestral state for the superclade Protostomia and both of its superphyla, Ecdysozoa and Lophotrochozoa, with high probability (>0.999). Within the Ecdysozoa, double-stranded was inferred as the ancestral state for six out of seven phyla included in the dataset (Kinorhyncha was the outlier), and we inferred five putative double-to-single transitions. The superphylum Lophotrochozoa exhibited by far the most rearranged mitogenomic architectures and the most complex scenario of strandedness transitions. Likely due to the highly rearranged mitogenomic architectures of most lineages, we failed to reconstruct of the ancestral architecture for this superphylum with precision, but multiple sources of evidence indicate that a double-stranded architecture was the ancestral state. These comprise most results of the ancestral architecture reconstruction (Figure S8), BayesTraits reconstruction (probability of double-stranded > 0.999), and the fact that double-stranded was the most likely ancestral state for 11 out of 13 individual phyla, with Brachiopoda and Syndermata as the only exceptions. Syndermata comprise sensu-stricto phyla Acanthocephala (all single-stranded) and Rotifera (mostly single-stranded) (Figures S9-S12). We found indications of single-stranded to double-stranded transitions in several species of Rotifera, but due to their fragmented mitogenomes, within-species strandedness variability, and strand switches comprising only tRNA genes, these are not confirmed. Another double-to-single transition was inferred in Platyhelminthes after Catenulida branched-off. Three lophotrochozoan phyla exhibited particularly complex scenarios: Bryozoa, Annelida, and Mollusca. In Annelida we identified a double-to-single evolutionary shift after Palaeoannelida branched-off, followed by a state reversal (i.e. single-to-double shift) in a single derived Sedentaria species, Sabella spalanzani (Sabellidae). Finally, Mollusca exhibited the most complex scenario, with multiple putative shifts in strandedness, comprising several putative state reversals observed in the class Bivalvia (Table 2).

GORR values distribution

Hypothesis 3: GORR values in comparison to the ancestral bilaterian architecture ranged between 0 and 12 in the complete dataset (Figures 1 and 2). The distribution of GORR values across individual phyla could be roughly classified into three basic, albeit not necessarily mutually exclusive, patterns of architectural evolution. (1) Discontinuous: in most phyla, the ancestral architecture (disregarding volatile tRNA genes) for the phylum is highly conserved in a majority of species, with exponentially elevated rearrangement rates in a small proportion of species (e.g. Arthropoda, Chordata, Nematoda, and Echinodermata). (2) Episodic: mitogenomic architecture is re-stabilised after an evolutionary period of increased levels of architectural rearrangements, commonly occurring deep in the evolutionary history (e.g. Nematoda and Arthropoda). (3) Continuous: GORR values exhibit an approximately linear distribution, characterised by the absence of statistical outliers. Most phyla exhibited a combination of episodic and discontinuous patterns, whereas Mollusca and Bryozoa were the only phyla exhibiting a continuous pattern. In addition, Platyhelminthes exhibited a unique pattern, with parasitic Neodermata exhibiting a strongly episodic pattern (exceptionally highly rearranged, but mostly stable architecture: GORR=9), and predominantly free-living “turbellaria” exhibiting much less rearranged, but fast-evolving in an apparently continuous manner, pattern of GORR distribution (Figure 2 and Supplementary Fig. 39).

GORR values, branch length, and strand distribution of genes

Hypothesis 4: Mitogenomic architectural evolutionary rates (GORR) strongly varied among the superphyla: highly conserved in Deuterostomia (0.24), intermediate in Ecdysozoa (3.29), and high in Lophotrochozoa (6.86). In support of the working hypothesis. branch lengths followed this pattern, but with less pronounced differences (Supplementary Fig. 40). Congruent patterns across the two variables were also observed across the individual phyla, with the slowest evolution in Chordata, Hemichordata, and Echinodermata, and fastest in Platyhelminthes, Orthonectida, and Mollusca/Acanthocephala (GORR/branch length respectively) (Figure 1 and 2, Supplementary Table 2). As a result, the correlation between GORR and branch length was strong and positive in the overall dataset (hypothesis 4a; r=0.69; p<0.001; Figure 3A), and branch length variability explained 37 - 40% of the GORR variability in Bilateria (Table 3). As Chordata exhibited a unique evolutionary pattern, and represented a majority of the dataset, major hypotheses were additionally tested with Chordata removed from the dataset: the overall conclusions remained the same, although the correlation value between GORR and branch length was slightly reduced (0.57). Correlation between GORR and branch length was also positive (albeit mostly weak) in all individual phyla aside from Mollusca (-0.08) (Figure 3), as well as in mitogenomes with low rearrangement rates (GORR<7; r=0.69, R2=42-45%; rejecting the hypothesis 4b), and in the dataset split along the lines of architectural type: single-stranded (r=0.86, R2=66-70%) and double-stranded (r=0.70, R2=47-49%). Contrary to this, highly rearranged mitogenomes (GORR≥7) exhibited a very weak negative correlation (-0.18) between GORR and branch length, reflected in low explanatory power (R2=3%), but the pattern was restored when Mollusca were removed from this dataset (r=0.71, R2=51%; further details in Table 3; Supplementary Note 4, Figs. 41 - 44, and Data 2).

Hypothesis 5: Next, we tested the hypothesis that mitogenomes with all genes encoded on the same strand are exhibit signatures of relaxed purifying selection pressures compared to double-stranded mitogenomes. In agreement with the working hypothesis 5a, GORR values were significantly higher in single-stranded mitogenomes across the Bilateria (Figure 4A; p<0.001, details in Supplementary Data 3). At the level of individual phyla, results were inconsistent, with Chordata and Arthropoda exhibiting a congruent pattern, but Annelida and Nematoda exhibiting an inverted GORR pattern (Figure 4A). In support of the hypothesis 5b, single-stranded mitogenomes exhibited significantly higher sequence evolutionary rates across the Bilateria (Figure 4B; p<0.001). At the level of individual phyla, results were only partially consistent, with single-stranded lineages exhibiting significantly longer branches in Chordata and Mollusca, nonsignificantly longer in Annelida and Arthropoda, and Nematoda exhibiting an inverted pattern (Figure 4B). Both hypotheses were also confirmed when Chordata were removed from the dataset (Supplementary Fig. 45).

As regards GC skews, mitogenomes with inverted (positive) values were observed in almost all phyla, aside from three phyla represented by only a few specimens: Entoprocta (n=2), Hemichordata (n=6), and Nematomorpha (n=1) (Figure 4C and Supplementary Fig. 46). GC skews were predominantly negative (the ancestral state) in double-stranded mitogenomes, and predominantly positive in single-stranded mitogenomes, but there were multiple exceptions from this rule, with Annelida as a major outlier (+ in ds, - in ss). In agreement with the hypothesis 5c, the absolute skew magnitude was significantly higher in single-stranded than in double-stranded mitogenomes (confirmed in both Bilateria - Figure 5A, and Chordata - Supplementary Fig. 47).

GC skews and Ne

Hypothesis 6: contrary to the working hypothesis 6a, GC skew (│value│>0.1) was negatively weakly correlated with GORR (r=-0.25), with a negligible explanatory power (R2≈3%). However, the working hypothesis was weakly-moderately supported when we separately analysed Chordata and the remaining Bilateria (both r=0.38; all p=<0.001), with higher explanatory power values (R2≈26-28% and 16-17% respectively). Hypothesis 5b was also rejected in the Bilateria dataset, where the correlation between GC skew and branch length was negligible (r=0.13, R2<1%), but supported when we separately analysed Chordata (r=0.37, R2≈20%) and the remaining Bilateria (r=0.50; R2≈28%; p=<0.001 in all cases; Supplementary Fig. 48).

Hypothesis 7: the Ne dataset comprised 202 species, belonging to four phyla: Chordata (182 species), Mollusca (9), Arthropoda (8), and Echinodermata (3). All were free living, but all three locomotory capacity categories were represented: 180 species in high, 14 in intermediate, and 9 in low. There were four single-stranded mitogenomes in the dataset. Contrary to the working hypotheses 7a-c, Ne was not correlated with GORR (r=0.07, p=0.30; R2=0.010), branch length (r=0.03, p=0.66; R2<0.006), and GC skew (r=-0.14, p=0.05; R2≈0.030). It was also not associated with strandedness (R2<0.030) and with skew inversions (R2<0.005) (Supplementary Fig. 49 and Data 2).

Parasitism, locomotory capacity, and thermoregulatory type

Hypothesis 8: In agreement with the working hypothesis 8a, endoparasitic species exhibited by far the most highly rearranged mitogenomic architectures, followed by ectoparasites, parasitoids, micropredators, and free-living species (Figure 5B). In pairwise comparisons, all differences were statistically significant (Tukey HSD tests; details in Supplementary Data 3), and Bayes factors were huge (Figure 6A, Figure S50). Statistical power was good and effect sizes were very large or huge for key pairwise comparisons: endoparasites vs. free-living (Cohen’s d=2.6), and ectoparasites vs. free-living (1.5) (Figure 6B). The results were replicated with Chordata removed from the dataset and across the Ecdysozoa and Lophotrochozoa (Supplementary Fig. 45). The patterns across the individual phyla were congruent in Platyhelminthes, and partially congruent in Arthropoda (elevated GORR in ectoparasites but not in endoparasites) and Nematoda (GORR was nonsignificantly increased in endoparasites) (Supplementary Fig. 51), and mixed across lower taxonomic levels (class and order): consistent in Insecta, Chromadorea, Malacostraca, Hexanauplia, and Rhabditida, but not in Arachnida, Enoplea, and Diptera (Supplementary Figs. 52 and 53). While lmekin and brms analyses indicated that the division along the lifestyle lines (parasitism) explained only around 6% of the variability in GORR in the bilaterian dataset, these values were higher once Chordata were excluded from the dataset: ≈33% in Ecdysozoa, ≈16% in Lophotrochozoa, and ≈20% in Protostomia (Table 3; Supplementary Data 2). To reduce the effect of variability in locomotory capacity, we focused only on the low locomotory capacity category divided along the lifestyle lines (hypothesis 8b). The pattern produced by the overall bilaterian dataset was only partially upheld, with the highest GORR values exhibited by endoparasites, but ectoparasites exhibited a lower value than free-living (Figure 5C). The explanatory power remained similar to the one in the full dataset (≈8%, Table 3).

Hypothesis 8c: in support of the working hypothesis, the far end of the positive GC skew distribution was marked by the strong prevalence of endoparasites: 24 species with highest skews were all endoparasites, and among the top 100 species with highest skews (GC range = 0.477 – 0.684), 93 were endoparasitic. A similar pattern was observed at the negative end of the GC skew distribution, where four highest values were exhibited by endoparasites (18 endoparasites in total in the GC-negative dataset). In partial agreement with these observations and the working hypothesis, absolute GC skews were the highest in endoparasites, but ectoparasites and parasitoids exhibited lower average values than the free-living species (Figure 5D, Supplementary Fig. S47). In support of hypothesis 8d, we found an increased likelihood (>37×) of skew inversions (positive GC skew) in macroparasitic (ectoparasitic+endoparasitic) species compared to free living (p<0.001, Fisher’s test, one-sided; Supplementary Fig. 54), with life history explaining 22% of the variability in skew direction (plus or minus).

Finally, in support of the hypothesis 8e, we found an increased likelihood of single-stranded mitogenomes in endoparasitic (>17×) and ectoparasitic (>3×) species , and decreased in other categories (<0.6× in free-living; Figure 7). Also, there was a highly significant association between life history and strandedness (p<0.001, Chi-square test of independence; Supplementary Data 3), with life history explaining 38-41% of the variability in the distribution of strand types across lineages (Table 3).

Hypothesis 9: in agreement with the working hypothesis 9a, GORR values were significantly increased in the low locomotory capacity category (Figure 5E). For the high vs. low category comparison, Bayes Factor was huge (Figure 6A, Supplementary Fig. 50), statistical power was good, and the effect size was huge (Cohen’s d=2.8; Figure 6C). The results were replicated with Chordata removed from the dataset and across all but one major taxonomic clades when both categories were present in sufficient numbers (n≥3): superphyla (Ecdysozoa+Lophotrochozoa), phyla (Chordata, Arthropoda, and Mollusca), and classes (Insecta, Malacostraca, and Arachnida) (insufficient data at the order level). The class Hexanauplia was the only major lineage where the hypothesis was rejected (Supplementary Figs. 45, 55, and 56). The explanatory power of locomotory capacity categorisation on GORR variability was ≈14% in Bilateria, ≈11% in Lophotrochozoa, and 33% in Ecdysozoa (Table 3). To remove the effect of parasitism on the locomotory capacity classification, we conducted analyses using only free-living species (hypothesis 9b). The pattern observed in the full dataset was mostly fully upheld (Figure 5F), and the explanatory power was ≈11% (Table 3). Among the ectoparasites (hypothesis 9c), those with low locomotory capacity had strongly (1.6×) but non-significantly increased GORR values (Figure 5G). In support of hypothesis 9d, GC skews were significantly increased in low-locomotory species (Figure 5H). In support of hypothesis 9e, there was an increased likelihood (>99×) of skew inversions (positive GC skew) in low-locomotory category compared to the high-locomotory category species (p<0.001, Fisher’s test, one-sided; Figure S54), and locomotory capacity explained 47% of the variability in skew direction. In support of hypothesis 9f, we found an increased likelihood (>3×) of single-stranded mitogenomes in species classified into the low locomotory capacity category, and decreased among the high-locomotory species (<0.4×, Figure 7, Supplementary Data 3). There was a highly significant association between the locomotory capacity and strandedness (p ≈ 0.0, Chi-square test of independence), with locomotory capacity explaining ≈33% of the variability in strand types across lineages (Table 3).

Hypothesis 10: in the bilaterian dataset 8,498 species were ectotherms, and 2,362 were endotherms (all Chordata and almost all free-living). Among the endotherms, >99% were classified in the high locomotory capacity category (none were low-locomotory). Among the ectotherms, ≈75% were high-locomotory, and ≈14% were low-locomotory. In agreement with the working hypotheses 10a/b, ectotherms exhibited significantly higher GORR (hypothesis 10a, Figure 5I), and branch lengths (hypothesis 10b, Figure 5J) than ectotherms, but Chordata exhibited an inverted pattern (Supplementary Fig. 45). The explanatory power of thermoregulatory type on these two variables was small: ≈2% and ≈5%, respectively (Table 3). Contrary to the working hypothesis 10c, endotherms exhibited significantly higher average GC skew value than ectotherms (both across the Bilateria and only Chordata; Figure 5K and Supplementary Fig. 47).

Mitogenome size patterns and correlates

Hypothesis 11: Aside from hypothesis 11i, all other hypotheses associated with correlates of mitogenomic size were rejected. Mitogenomes were the smallest (≈12.6 Kb) in Longidoridae (Nematoda: Enoplea), and the largest in two Bivalvia (Mollusca) species: Anadara sativa (48.2 Kb) and Dreissena rostriformis (46.7 Kb). Only eight species exhibited mitogenomes >30 Kb (5 Mollusca and 3 Arthropoda). Multiple Chordata species (Squamata and Anura) were among the largest mitogenomes (>25 Kb) (Supplementary Data 1). The correlation between GORR and mitogenome size was weakly/moderately negative in Bilateria (hypothesis 11a; r=-0.39, Figure 3B), and size explained ≈10% of the GORR variability (Table 3). In individual phyla, correlation between GORR and size was highly variable: positive in Annelida, Echinodermata, and Nematoda (weak – moderate); negative in Platyhelminthes and Mollusca (weak); and negligible in Arthropoda, Chordata, and Bilateria (Figure 3B, Supplementary Fig. 57). The correlation between mitogenome size and branch length was weakly negative across the bilaterian dataset (hypothesis 11b, r=-0.33, Figure 3C). It also varied across the individual phyla: positive in Mollusca, Nematoda, Echinodermata, and Annelida (weak – moderate); negative in Arthropoda and Platyhelminthes (negligible – weak); and negligible in Chordata and Bilateria (Figure 3C, Supplementary Fig. 57). Ne values were not correlated with size (hypothesis 11c, r=-0.09, p=0.21, R2<0.013, Supplementary Fig. 49). GC skew was also negligibly correlated with size across all tested datasets (hypothesis 11d, r≈-0.07 - 0.17; R2≈0.005 - 0.030; Table 3, Supplementary Fig. 48). Mitogenomes were the largest in free-living, and the smallest in ectoparasitic and endoparasitic lineages (hypothesis 11e, Figure 5L). Mitogenomes were larger in high-locomotory than in low-locomotory categories (hypothesis 11f, Figure 5M). Double-stranded mitogenomes were larger than single-stranded ones (hypothesis 11g, Figure 5N). Endotherms had larger mitogenomes than ectotherms (hypothesis 11h, Figure 5O). Finally, in agreement with hypothesis 11i, variability in size was lesser in endotherms than in ectotherms (SD = 537 vs. 1340, respectively, Figure 5O).

## Methods

Dataset, categorisation, phylogeny, branch lengths, and Ne

Features of all mitogenomes of bilaterian animals available in the NCBI’s manually curated RefSeq database were extracted, calculated, and comparative tables generated using PhyloSuite 75,76. The dataset was categorised according to the lifestyle (endoparasites, ectoparasites, parasitoids, micropredators, and free-living species), locomotory capacity (high, intermediate, and low), and thermoregulatory type (endotherms and ectotherms). Duplicated genes were resolved using PhyloSuite following the methodology described previously 10,75. To infer branch lengths, we used the phylogeny from our previous study 10, reconstructed using concatenated amino acid sequences of 12 mitochondrial protein-coding genes (atp8 removed) of all mitogenomes in the dataset, and mtZOA+G4+F+C50 model in IQ-TREE v2.2.0.7.mix 77. We constrained the phylum-level topology according to the bilaterian phylogeny in Laumer et al.78, with Xenacoelomorpha as the sister lineage to all other bilaterians 79,80 (“Nephrozoa” topology henceforth). The molecular sequence evolution rate was defined as the root-to-tip branch lengths, which were extracted using the TreeSuite function in PhyloSuite. More details about the dataset, including the limitations of these classifications, and methodology are available in Supplementary Methods and in Jakovlić et al.10. The effective population size (Ne) analyses were extracted by overlapping the species in our dataset with those in the dataset recently compiled by Clarke et al.81. When there were multiple populations per species, we inferred average Ne values.

GC skews

To exclude the confounding factor of variability in the noncoding region size, GC skews were calculated 82 by PhyloSuite using only coding sections of the plus strand (GC skew is more pronounced than AT skew and thus more suitable for testing these hypotheses). To attempt to reduce the amount of noise in the GC skew dataset stemming from inversions in mutational pressures caused by inversions of the origin of replication 35,36 and facilitate the analysis of magnitude irrespective of skew direction, all GC skews were converted to their absolute values. To further reduce the amount of noise, the lower end of distribution (GC<0.1) was removed, as such low GC values commonly suggest ORI inversions or otherwise disrupted replication mechanisms, so they poorly reflect the strength of purifying selection pressure 36. In addition, we attempted to remove all annotation artefacts caused by the authors submitting the wrong mitogenomic strand to the GenBank via a manual inspection of the dataset (removed 65 species).

Mitogenomic architecture analyses

Mitogenomes of bilaterian animals commonly encode 37 genes (13 protein-coding genes - PCGs, 2 rRNAs, and 22 tRNAs) distributed in varying arrangements across both DNA strands, by convention named “plus” and “minus”. This arrangement is referred to as mitogenomic architecture, and it can be quantified as the gene order rearrangement rate (GORR). For the ancestral architecture inference, we relied on previous proposals of ancestral architectures for different lineages (Supplementary Table 3), and conducted the ancestral mitogenomic architecture inference using TreeREx 83 and MLGO 84 using a linearised gene order dataset from which tRNAs were removed due to their highly variable content and difficulties in annotation. To minimise the noise and reduce the size of dataset (362 species after the reduction), we used only the ancestral architecture for a phylum when it was inferred with confidence by previous studies (e.g. only the mitogenome of Homo sapiens for Chordata 5,30 and Limulus polyphemus for Arthropoda 85), and only the “basal” lineage of large phyla exhibiting high rearrangement rates (e.g. only Catenulida for Platyhelminthes 57). As the phylogeny of Bilateria remain debated, we tested two topologies, both constrained at the phylum level. Aside from the “Nephrozoa” topology, described in the first section, we also tested the topology where Xenacoelomorpha is the sister group to Ambulacraria (Hemichordata+Echinodermata) 86,87, with paraphyletic Deuterostomia 88 - named “Xenambulacraria” henceforth. As this topology implies that the common ancestor of Chordata and Xenambulacraria (Ambulacraria+Xenacoelomorpha) was the last common ancestor of all Bilateria, and characters common to these two clades would be bilaterian plesiomorphies 88, we removed the highly rearranged Protostomia (Ecdysozoa and Lophotrochozoa) 5,30, and tested a dataset comprising only the outgroups, Xenambulacraria, and Chordata, constrained according to the relationships proposed previously 86,88. The outgroups were Cnidaria, Porifera, and Placozoa. Further methodological details are provided in Supplementary Methods. The inferred ur-bilaterian mitogenomic architecture (tRNAs excluded) was then used to calculate mitogenomic GORR values using the Breakpoint Distance measure in CREX 89. As TreeREx and CREX cannot handle missing genes, for these analyses, atp8 was removed from all mitogenomes, and species with further missing PCGs or rRNAs were removed from these analyses, which included the entire phylum Chaetognatha - lacking atp6 2,90. In addition, all mitogenomes were classified into two categories according to the strand distribution of genes: double-stranded (genes encoded on both strands) and single-stranded (all genes encoded on a single strand), and then the Maximum Likelihood method in BayesTraits v4.0.1 91 was used to infer the ancestral states of strand distribution of genes. To get a better resolution for strandedness analyses, we further analysed complete GenBank mitogenomic datasets (as opposed to only RefSeq) for all poorly represented major lineages, and for all lineages with complex evolutionary histories.

Statistical analyses

As GORR values equalled 0 for more than half of the dataset, mostly due to a majority of Chordata having a perfectly conserved ancestral bilaterian architecture and being overrepresented in the dataset (>50% of all species), we recoded GORR=0 values to 0.0000001 for all statistical analyses. To further confirm that Chordata did not skew our statistical analyses, we additionally tested all major hypotheses using a bilaterian dataset from which all Chordata were removed. Outliers in GORR distributions were identified using the IQR method (InterQuartile Range), selected due to the non-normality of GORR distribution. Pairwise comparisons of between different groups were conducted using Tukey HSD tests in the R package agricolae v1.3.5 92. As the limitations of the traditional p-value-based statistics are well-documented, we further assessed the reliability of statistical analyses by employing multiple recommended alternative tests 93. Effect sizes were inferred using the R package efsize. Statistical power analyses were conducted for each effect size measure using the pwr.t2n.test method in the R package pwr. Herein, power refers to the probability of detecting a statistically significant effect if one exists, and the commonly accepted cut-off value for a good statistical power is ≥ 0.8. Bayesian hypothesis testing was conducted using BayesFactor 94. As the dataset violated the assumption of independence of data, two algorithms designed to account for phylogenetic relatedness were used to conduct multilevel linear regression analyses: linear fixed-effect models accounting for kinship implemented in the lmekin function in coxme v2.2.16 95, and phylogenetic multilevel Bayesian models implemented in brms v2.16.150 96. For these analyses, we used a matrix of phylogenetic distances extracted from the phylogenetic tree described above using the ape v5.5 package 97. The R2 value of lmekin models was calculated using the r.squaredLR method available in the MuMIn v1.46.0 package in R. The Bayesian R2 value was inferred using the bayes_r2 function of brms package in R. For brms and lmekin analyses, we log-transformed the obtained GORR data to reduce the non-normality of distribution. Pearson’s correlation coefficients (r) were inferred using R. Correlation values were classified as follows: negligible (<0.2), weak (0.2-0.4), moderate (0.4-0.6), strong (0.6-0.8), very strong (>0.8). Due to the very large number of samples in our study (>10,000), we did not rely on p-values to assess the support for the working hypotheses in correlation tests, as statistical tests are practically always highly significant on such high numbers of samples 98. Unless if specified otherwise, statistical tests were inherently two-sided.

Categorisation of locomotory capacity
The categorisation of locomotory capacity was based on the “visual interaction hypothesis”, which is the best explanatory
variable for variability in scaling coefficients between the mass-specific metabolic rate in marine animals: high metabolic
demand follows strong selection for locomotory capacity for pursuit and evasion in visual prey/predators inhabiting well-lit
oceanic waters, whereas limited visibility allows for reduced locomotory capacity, reflected in low metabolic rates
(Childress and Mickel 1985; Seibel and Drazen 2007). We divided the dataset into three locomotory capacity categories: (1)
High comprised all species expected to rely on locomotion for pursuit and evasion of prey/predators. This category
comprised a vast majority of species (8,713); (2) Low comprised all species that have merely a rudimentary locomotory
capacity. This comprises sedentary species, or those capable only of minimal, very slow locomotion, that do not rely on
locomotion for pursuit and evasion of prey/predators. This category comprised 1,202 species, mostly from lineages such as
nematodes, flatworms, sessile molluscs and crustaceans, parasitic crustaceans, ticks, some annelids, mites,
Acanthocephala, Diplura, Brachiopoda, Bryozoa, Ascidiacea, Echinodermata, Entoprocta, Gastrotricha, Gnathostomulida,
Hemichordata, Kinorhyncha, Nemertea, Onychophora, Orthonectida, Phoronida, Priapulida, Tardigrada, and
Xenacoelomorpha; (3) Because locomotory capacity is a continuous trait, it is impossible to categorise species into only two
categories without creating a large overlap between the two categories. Therefore, to minimise the overlap between the
Low and High locomotory capacity categories, we designed a third category: Intermediate locomotory capacity. This
category comprised 945 species that would be expected to possess more than a rudimentary locomotory capacity, but also
rely on strategies other than locomotion to evade/pursue predators/prey. Examples are certain flightless insects and
Collembola, certain bathyal, abyssal and stygobitic crustacean and fish lineages, Chaetognatha, certain amphibian and
reptilian lineages, some mammals, some Bivalvia and Cephalopoda, some Gastropoda, Nematomorpha, and Rotifera.
Certain lineages were rather difficult to classify. Chaetognaths swim in short bursts using a dorso-ventral undulating body
motion, where their tail fin assists with propulsion and the body fins with stabilization and steering, so we classified them
into the Intermediate category. Among the Annelida, Sipuncula merely have a rudimentary LOC, so they were classified as
Low. Crassiclitellata (earthworms), Hirudinida (leeches) and Eunicida are capable of more than rudimentary locomotion, so
we classified them as Intermediate. Sabellida are sedentary, so we classified them as Low. Terebellida and Urechidae
appear to possess merely a rudimentary locomotory capacity, so we placed them into the Low category. Magelonidae are
burrowing worms with limited mobility, so we classified them as Low. Among the Nemertea, some species may possess
more than a basic locomotory capacity, but due to limited evidence, we classified them all as Low. Phoronida, Priapulida,
Entoprocta, and Hemichordata possess merely a rudimentary locomotory capacity, so all were classified as Low.
Onychophora can move at up to 5 cm per second, so we classified them as Intermediate.
